---
id: c-sensor-ring
title: Sensor Ring Buffer and Monotonic Stack
difficulty: Medium
order: 1
tags: circular buffer, stack, monotonic stack, embedded
---
## Statement
Two components every robot firmware needs:

**1. A fixed-capacity ring buffer** of `float` sensor samples that **overwrites the oldest** sample when full (keep the last N readings), with no `malloc` after `ring_init`:

```c
typedef struct { float *buf; size_t cap, head, count; } Ring;
int    ring_init(Ring *r, size_t cap);          /* the only allocation; cap must be a power of two, else return -1 */
void   ring_free(Ring *r);
void   ring_push(Ring *r, float x);             /* overwrite the oldest when full */
int    ring_pop(Ring *r, float *out);           /* oldest first; -1 if empty */
size_t ring_size(const Ring *r);
float  ring_get(const Ring *r, size_t i);       /* i-th oldest (0 = oldest); i < size */
float  ring_mean(const Ring *r);                /* mean of the current contents (0 if empty) */
```

**2. `next_greater`:** for each sample in an array, the distance (in samples) to the next **strictly greater** sample, or 0 if none. Implement it in **O(n)** with a monotonic stack of indices. (It's used to find "time until the next spike" in sensor logs.)

```c
void next_greater(const float *a, size_t n, int *out);
```

## Starter
```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

typedef struct { float *buf; size_t cap, head, count; } Ring;

int ring_init(Ring *r, size_t cap) { return -1; }
void ring_free(Ring *r) {}
void ring_push(Ring *r, float x) {}
int ring_pop(Ring *r, float *out) { return -1; }
size_t ring_size(const Ring *r) { return 0; }
float ring_get(const Ring *r, size_t i) { return 0; }
float ring_mean(const Ring *r) { return 0; }

void next_greater(const float *a, size_t n, int *out) {
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        out[i] = 0;
        for (size_t j = i + 1; j < n; j++) if (a[j] > a[i]) { out[i] = (int)(j - i); break; }
    }
}
```

## Driver
```c
#include <string.h>

int main(void) {
    char cmd[16];
    Ring r = {0};
    while (scanf("%15s", cmd) == 1) {
        if (strcmp(cmd, "init") == 0) {
            size_t c; scanf("%zu", &c);
            ring_free(&r);
            printf("init %zu -> %d\n", c, ring_init(&r, c));
        } else if (strcmp(cmd, "push") == 0) {
            int k; scanf("%d", &k);
            for (int i = 0; i < k; i++) { float x; scanf("%f", &x); ring_push(&r, x); }
        } else if (strcmp(cmd, "pop") == 0) {
            float x;
            if (ring_pop(&r, &x) == 0) printf("pop %.2f\n", x); else printf("pop empty\n");
        } else if (strcmp(cmd, "show") == 0) {
            printf("size %zu mean %.3f [", ring_size(&r), ring_mean(&r));
            for (size_t i = 0; i < ring_size(&r); i++) printf(i ? " %.1f" : "%.1f", ring_get(&r, i));
            printf("]\n");
        } else if (strcmp(cmd, "ng") == 0) {
            size_t n; scanf("%zu", &n);
            float *a = malloc((n ? n : 1) * sizeof *a);
            int *o = malloc((n ? n : 1) * sizeof *o);
            for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) scanf("%f", &a[i]);
            next_greater(a, n, o);
            long long sum = 0;
            int maxd = 0;
            for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) { sum += o[i]; if (o[i] > maxd) maxd = o[i]; }
            if (n <= 20) { printf("ng:"); for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) printf(" %d", o[i]); printf("\n"); }
            printf("ng sum %lld max %d\n", sum, maxd);
            free(a); free(o);
        }
    }
    ring_free(&r);
    return 0;
}
```

## Hints
- With `cap` a power of two, wrap indices with `& (cap - 1)`. Check it with `cap && !(cap & (cap - 1))`.
- Push when full: write at `(head + count) & mask`, which is the oldest slot, then advance `head`.
- `ring_get(i)` is `buf[(head + i) & mask]`.
- Monotonic stack: walk the array, and while the stack's top index has a smaller value than `a[i]`, pop it and set `out[top] = i - top`. Then push `i`. Whatever is left on the stack gets 0. Each index is pushed and popped once, so it's O(n).

## Solution
```c
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdlib.h>

typedef struct { float *buf; size_t cap, head, count; } Ring;

int ring_init(Ring *r, size_t cap) {
    r->buf = NULL;
    r->cap = r->head = r->count = 0;
    if (cap == 0 || (cap & (cap - 1))) return -1;    /* must be a power of two */
    r->buf = malloc(cap * sizeof *r->buf);
    if (!r->buf) return -1;
    r->cap = cap;
    return 0;
}

void ring_free(Ring *r) { free(r->buf); r->buf = NULL; r->cap = r->head = r->count = 0; }

void ring_push(Ring *r, float x) {
    if (!r->cap) return;
    size_t mask = r->cap - 1;
    r->buf[(r->head + r->count) & mask] = x;
    if (r->count == r->cap) r->head = (r->head + 1) & mask;   /* overwrote the oldest */
    else r->count++;
}

int ring_pop(Ring *r, float *out) {
    if (r->count == 0) return -1;
    *out = r->buf[r->head];
    r->head = (r->head + 1) & (r->cap - 1);
    r->count--;
    return 0;
}

size_t ring_size(const Ring *r) { return r->count; }
float ring_get(const Ring *r, size_t i) { return r->buf[(r->head + i) & (r->cap - 1)]; }

float ring_mean(const Ring *r) {
    if (r->count == 0) return 0;
    double s = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < r->count; i++) s += ring_get(r, i);
    return (float)(s / (double)r->count);
}

void next_greater(const float *a, size_t n, int *out) {
    size_t *stack = malloc((n ? n : 1) * sizeof *stack);
    size_t top = 0;
    for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
        out[i] = 0;
        while (top > 0 && a[stack[top - 1]] < a[i]) {   /* a[i] answers every smaller pending index */
            size_t j = stack[--top];
            out[j] = (int)(i - j);
        }
        stack[top++] = i;                               /* indices on the stack have decreasing values */
    }
    free(stack);
}
```

- **The ring buffer** never shifts or reallocates: push and pop are a few integer operations, ideal for ISRs and fixed-memory systems. "Overwrite the oldest" keeps a sliding window of the latest N samples, and power-of-two capacities make the wrap a single AND.
- **The monotonic stack** turns an O(n²) search into O(n): the stack holds indices still waiting for a greater value, in decreasing order of value, and each new sample resolves every smaller waiting index at once. On 300 000 descending samples the naive version does about 4.5·10¹⁰ comparisons, while the stack does 300 000 pushes.
